summary.text: At \(n=140\), squaring bounds show that the relevant \(\lfloor m\sqrt{5/4}\rfloor\) values for \(m=140,144,157,161\) are respectively \(156,160,175,180\), giving \(a(140)=471\), \(a(144)=484\), \(a(157)=528\), and \(a(161)=542\). Thus the claimed relation would require \(542=528+484-471=541\), so it fails.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=2n+\left\lfloor n\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac n4\right\rfloor
\qquad(n\ge 1).
\]
We disprove the proposed identity
\[
a(n+21)=a(n+17)+a(n+4)-a(n)
\]
by evaluating both sides at \(n=140\).

We first record how the irrational floor terms will be evaluated without using decimal approximations. Since
\[
\sqrt{\frac54}=\frac{\sqrt5}{2}>0,
\]
for nonnegative integers \(n,k\), the two inequalities
\[
4k^2\le 5n^2<4(k+1)^2
\]
imply
\[
k\le n\sqrt{\frac54}<k+1.
\]
Indeed, all quantities involved are nonnegative, so each comparison can be squared without changing its direction: the first displayed inequality is exactly the squared form of
\(k\le n\sqrt{5/4}\), and the second is exactly the squared form of
\(n\sqrt{5/4}<k+1\). Consequently,
\[
\left\lfloor n\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=k.
\]
We apply this criterion separately to the four indices appearing when \(n=140\), namely \(140,144,157,161\).

For \(n=140\), take \(k=156\). The exact comparisons are
\[
4\cdot156^2=97{,}344
\le 98{,}000=5\cdot140^2
<98{,}596=4\cdot157^2.
\]
Thus
\[
\left\lfloor140\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=156.
\]
Also \(\lfloor140/4\rfloor=35\). Hence
\[
a(140)=2\cdot140+156+35=471.
\]

For \(n=144\), take \(k=160\). We have
\[
4\cdot160^2=102{,}400
\le 103{,}680=5\cdot144^2
<103{,}684=4\cdot161^2.
\]
Therefore
\[
\left\lfloor144\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=160.
\]
Since \(\lfloor144/4\rfloor=36\), it follows that
\[
a(144)=2\cdot144+160+36=484.
\]

For \(n=157\), take \(k=175\). The relevant integer inequalities are
\[
4\cdot175^2=122{,}500
\le 123{,}245=5\cdot157^2
<123{,}904=4\cdot176^2.
\]
Thus
\[
\left\lfloor157\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=175.
\]
Moreover, \(157=4\cdot39+1\), so \(\lfloor157/4\rfloor=39\). Consequently,
\[
a(157)=2\cdot157+175+39=528.
\]

Finally, for \(n=161\), take \(k=180\). We have
\[
4\cdot180^2=129{,}600
\le 129{,}605=5\cdot161^2
<131{,}044=4\cdot181^2.
\]
It follows that
\[
\left\lfloor161\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=180.
\]
As \(161=4\cdot40+1\), we also have \(\lfloor161/4\rfloor=40\), and hence
\[
a(161)=2\cdot161+180+40=542.
\]

Now substitute \(n=140\) into the conjectured recurrence. Its left-hand side is
\[
a(140+21)=a(161)=542.
\]
Its right-hand side is
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(140+17)+a(140+4)-a(140)
&=a(157)+a(144)-a(140)\\
&=528+484-471\\
&=541.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the proposed equality at \(n=140\) would assert \(542=541\), which is false. Since \(140\ge1\), this is an admissible index in the universal claim. Therefore the conjecture that
\(a(n+21)=a(n+17)+a(n+4)-a(n)\) for every \(n\ge1\) is disproved.
